questions.prompt: With exact line search, successive steepest-descent directions are orthogonal because
questions.explanation: Exact line search makes the new gradient orthogonal to the step just taken. For steepest descent that step is the negative of the old gradient, so the new gradient is orthogonal to the old one. The next steepest direction, the negative of the new gradient, is therefore orthogonal to the previous direction. The Hessian need not be a multiple of the identity. That special case actually finishes in one step. The step length is not constantly 1, and orthogonal directions are not parallel.

questions.prompt: On a long, thin elliptical level set, steepest descent zigzags because
questions.explanation: The negative gradient is perpendicular to the level set. On a very elongated ellipse that perpendicular hits the opposite side quickly, and the new perpendicular is almost a reversal. The gradient changes from point to point on an ellipse. Exact line search makes consecutive steepest steps orthogonal, not parallel. Equal eigenvalues make the level sets round, and one exact steepest step reaches the center.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that shows successive steepest directions are orthogonal. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The line search is what produces a zero derivative, and that derivative is the new orthogonality relation. Identifying the step with the old negative gradient turns orthogonality to the step into orthogonality of the two gradients. The next direction is defined from the new gradient, so it inherits that right angle. Claiming the directions are orthogonal before the line search has set the derivative skips the only fact that forces the angle.

questions.prompt: Which of these pairs of successive steepest directions are orthogonal?
questions.explanation:
Orthogonality is a zero dot product.
• \((-1, 2)\cdot(2, 1) = -2 + 2 = 0\).
• \((1, 1)\cdot(1, -1) = 1 - 1 = 0\).
• \((3, -1)\cdot(1, 3) = 3 - 3 = 0\).
• \((2, 0)\cdot(1, 1) = 2\).
• \((1, 2)\cdot(2, 2) = 6\).
The last two pairs are not orthogonal.

questions.prompt: The Hessian is \(p\) times the identity, and the nonzero gradient is \((u, v)\). The exact steepest-descent step length equals
questions.explanation: The general steepest step is \(\lVert g\rVert^2 / (g^T A g)\). With \(A = p I\), the denominator is \(p(u^2 + v^2)\), so the ratio collapses to \(1/p\). All three names appear before that cancellation. Leaving \(p\) out of the denominator is the step for the identity Hessian. Using \(p\) in the numerator inverts the step. The product \(u v\) is not the squared norm.

questions.prompt: A note explains the turn in steepest descent. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: Exact line search gives \(\nabla f(x^+)^T d = 0\), and \(d = -\nabla f(x)\) turns that into orthogonality of successive gradients. Conjugacy of two directions is \(d_i^T A d_j = 0\). Euclidean orthogonality is \(d_i^T d_j = 0\). Those agree for every positive definite \(A\) only when \(A\) is a multiple of the identity. In that special case the method finishes in one step. In general, orthogonality does not give the finite termination that conjugacy gives, so the last step stands.

steps: Exact line search makes the new gradient orthogonal to the step just taken.
For steepest descent that step is the negative gradient, so successive gradients are orthogonal.
Euclidean orthogonality of those gradients is the same as conjugacy with respect to every positive definite Hessian.
Without conjugacy, steepest descent need not reach the minimizer in \(n\) steps.
reasons: Conjugacy is \(d_i^T A d_j = 0\). Euclidean orthogonality does not include \(A\).
Exact line search does not make the new gradient orthogonal to the step.
Steepest descent with exact line search reaches every quadratic minimizer in one step, in every dimension.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \mathrm{diag}(2, 6)\) and start steepest descent with exact line search at \(x = (3, 1)\), where the gradient is \((6, 6)\). The step length is \(1/4\), and the next point is \((3/2, -1/2)\). What is the squared Euclidean norm of the new gradient?
questions.explanation: The new gradient is \(A\) times the new point, \((2 \cdot 3/2,\ 6 \cdot (-1/2)) = (3, -3)\). Its squared norm is \(9 + 9 = 18\). The old gradient \((6, 6)\) dots with \((3, -3)\) to give 0, which is the orthogonality this step is built on. Reporting \(72\) repeats the old squared norm. Reporting \(9\) is only one of the two squares. Reporting \(0\) is that dot product, not the squared norm.

questions.prompt: The zigzag becomes more severe when the condition number of the Hessian grows, because
questions.explanation: A large ratio of extreme eigenvalues stretches the elliptical level sets. The geometry of the perpendicular steps then folds into a tight zigzag, and the contraction factor moves toward 1. Equal eigenvalues make circles, which are the mild case. The exact step for a fixed gradient stays finite. Orthogonality of successive gradients holds for every positive definite Hessian, including a well-conditioned one.

successive gradients stop being orthogonal

questions.prompt: The linear rate that measures this zigzag on a quadratic is a function of
questions.explanation: The excess contracts by at most \(((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1))^2\). The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues, and two Hessians with the same trace can have very different ratios. The starting value scales the excess and does not set the factor. Sparsity of the first gradient is an accident of the coordinates.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \mathrm{diag}(1, 5)\) and start at \(x = (5, 1)\), where the gradient is \((5, 5)\). What exact steepest-descent step length is taken?
questions.explanation: The squared gradient norm is \(50\). Then \(A \nabla f = (5, 25)\) and the curvature is \(25 + 125 = 150\). The step is \(50/150 = 1/3\). Reporting \(3\) inverts the ratio. Reporting \(150\) is the curvature. Reporting \(1\) would require the curvature to equal the squared norm, which would mean \(A\) is the identity on the span of the gradient.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Conjugate directions improve on this zigzag by replacing Euclidean orthogonality with
questions.explanation: Conjugacy uses the Hessian in the inner product. On a positive definite quadratic, a set of \(n\) conjugate directions with exact line search reaches the minimizer in at most \(n\) steps. Repeating one direction cannot span the space. The condition number is not a step length. The line search is still what picks the coefficient of each direction.
